_contract: Shared Go/TS accept-set parity fixture for approved private software-download origins.
Read by BOTH sides of the seam:
Go: agent/internal/netpolicy/origin_parity_test.go
TS: packages/shared/src/validators/softwareDownloadPolicy.parity.test.ts
Fields:
origin        - the raw string an operator could type into the allowlist.
goAcceptsRaw  - whether netpolicy.parseOrigin(origin) succeeds. Recorded for
documentation; it is NOT the safety property (Go legitimately
accepts strings the HTTPS-only TS schema refuses, e.g. http://
or a loopback literal, because parseOrigin does not classify
addresses -- that happens at dial time).
tsNormalized  - the exact value normalizePrivateSoftwareOrigin must return, or
null when it must reject.
THE LOAD-BEARING INVARIANT, asserted by the Go test: for every case with a
non-null tsNormalized, netpolicy.parseOrigin(tsNormalized) must SUCCEED. That is
the accept-set subset property. Violating it is not a cosmetic divergence: the
agent's netpolicy.NewClient aborts on the FIRST unparseable configured origin,
so a single validator-blessed row the agent cannot parse denies an entire
org/site every managed-software install -- including public-CDN installs that
need no allowlist entry at all. (The agent also degrades to an empty approved
set rather than failing outright now; this fixture keeps the validator from
producing the input that degradation exists to survive.)
When adding a host spelling to either side's rules, add a case here FIRST.

cases.note: the ordinary case: a customer-hosted repository name
explicit non-default port survives normalization on both sides
case and trailing root dot both normalize away, identically
RFC1918 literal: exactly what this allowlist exists to approve
RFC1918 literal with a port
CGNAT is classPrivate on the Go side, not forbidden
ULA literal, the IPv6 counterpart of RFC1918
bracketed ULA literal keeps its brackets and port
canonical IPv6 text form
a public literal is storable; it simply grants nothing extra
OVER-REJECTION GUARD: all-hex-letter name, no 0x marker, so isNumericLookingHost must say no on both sides
OVER-REJECTION GUARD: only separator/marker characters but no digit, so isNumericLookingHost must say no (hasDigit rule)
C1: exactly how a tech writes a subnet. The WHATWG parser keeps it as a DNS name, so nothing but isNumericLookingHost rejects it
C1: same shape, two wildcard labels
C1: hex shorthand whose trailing label kept the URL parser from resolving it to an address; rejected only because a 0x marker is present
C1: mixed hex shorthand
five numeric labels: the URL parser refuses it outright, Go's isNumericLookingHost catches it
empty label is not a valid DNS name and would be a forbidden-hostname bypass spelling
IPv4-mapped is rejected unconditionally on both sides; write https://10.0.0.5 instead
port 0 is out of range for both
userinfo is refused by both
decimal shorthand for 127.0.0.1: Go rejects the shape, TS canonicalizes then rejects the loopback range. Different reason, same answer
octal shorthand for 127.0.0.1
short-form shorthand for 127.0.0.1
TS-STRICTER: parseOrigin does not classify addresses (that is dial time), so Go parses this happily; the validator refuses to store a loopback origin at all
TS-STRICTER: same reason -- Go's forbidden-hostname check is at dial time, not in parseOrigin
TS-STRICTER: Alibaba metadata inside the otherwise-allowed CGNAT range
TS-STRICTER: Go accepts http for a configured CONTROL-PLANE origin; an approved software origin is HTTPS-only
TS-STRICTER: parseOrigin discards the path; the validator refuses it so a stored entry cannot look like a prefix rule
TS-STRICTER: Go's checkHostShape has no opinion on '*' (nothing would ever match the literal name at dial time); the validator refuses it so nobody stores a wildcard believing it works

DOCUMENTED CANONICALIZATION: Go rejects the raw hex shorthand, but the value the validator STORES is the canonical dotted quad, which Go accepts -- so the subset property holds on what actually crosses the wire. The raw form never reaches the agent

DOCUMENTED CANONICALIZATION, and a footgun: the WHATWG parser reads the leading zero as octal, so an operator who meant 10.0.0.5 stores PUBLIC 8.0.0.5. Storable and parseable by both sides -- it just does not approve what they intended
DOCUMENTED CANONICALIZATION: Go rejects non-canonical IPv6 text, but the stored value is the canonical form (the WHATWG serializer compresses the longest zero run exactly as netip.Addr.String does)
